articles.title: A new dark age?
articles.content: RECENT years have seen a surge of books and articles on the impact of technology on people’s lives and thinking. While communication technology has opened new vistas and opportunities it has also created its own problems in our digital age. Some works celebrate its benefits. Others warn of its damaging consequences especially those of social media. James Marriott’sThe New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Societyjoins this debate from another angle. The British journalist’s work falls within the genre that emphasises the harmful consequences of digital technology. The book’s principal concern is that people aren’t reading anymore and that a screen culture is displacing a print culture. For Marriott, the spread of literacy and the kind of thinking nurtured by the world of print drove progress in economic development, scientific advancement, and the emergence of modern democracy. In a print culture, he argues, knowledge is organised, understood, and contextualised. “Books make arguments, propose theses and develop ideas.” This process, he contends, develops the power of reasoning. For Marriott, this is getting lost in an era where the smartphone has taken over our lives and become the main reason for the decline of reading. There has never been a technology quite like the smartphone, which has so much distracting content that it keeps people’s attention endlessly on the screen. He maintains that a hostile environment for learning has been created by this digital distraction. Screens are changing human behaviour. Smartphones are shaping a “fragmented, trivialised and angry new world”, in which conspiracy theories and mad ideas are spread at terrifying speed. The spread of knowledge is impeded by this and is actually breaking down. Political discourse once grounded in logical argument now takes place “amid the moronic inferno of social media”. Marriot attributes much of the 21st century’s disorder and unreason to the fading of the written word and the “colonisation of culture” by addictive screens. He sees the intellectual hollowing of society as a consequence of the decline of reading and the world becoming a less rational place. Public discourse today, he claims, has become trivial to the point of dysfunction. It has affected politics too as this environment encourages the rise of mediocre politicians with little understanding of history, whose appeals to the public are emotional and do not rest on rational propositions. Politics, Marriott argues, is growing “angrier, stupider and more obsessed with personality”. He laments the fact that the full ramifications of the onset of what he calls a post-literate society are not fully understood. Marriot may be overstating his case and exaggerating the damaging impact of digital technology. But he is no outlier in this assessment. Last year in a compelling bookSuperbloom: How Technologies of Connection Tear Us Apart, Nicholas Carr surveyed how digital technology — including smartphones, the internet, social media and artificial intelligence — is transforming both people and societies. He argued that instead of broadening minds, expanding empathy and fostering harmony, this technology has had the opposite effect. It is eroding understanding and trust and contributing to strife and social disharmony. Communication technology offers immense opportunities but has serious unintended consequences. For Carr, speed and intensity in the flow of information and stimuli compel people to rely on intuitive thinking based on biases. It deprives them of the ability to tap into deeper analysis. As a result, it has undermined reasoned analysis, methodical evaluation and contemplative inquiry. As he puts it “Attention splinters, understanding grows thin”. This results in mental shortcuts and shallow thinking. Thus “rather than levelling barriers to knowledge, it becomes a barrier itself”. For both Marriott and Carr, the information spread through digital vehicles does not foster knowledge but detracts from it. “More informed does not mean better informed.” The fragmented nature of information provided by the screen makes much of it useless, according to Marriott. Social media further dumbs down the public conversation. Marriott sees social media and short-form videos producing junk content and misleading posts. He also finds a connection between video platforms like TikTok and increased vote share for populist and far right parties. That’s because feeds by such parties play on emotions and abjure reasoning. Carr’s book devotes far more attention to social media. His criticism is unsparing. He also takes tech companies to task. In his view, social media amplifies falsehoods and hostility rather than promote facts and truth. Because it is shorn of communication barriers, it brings out people’s worst instincts. He also blames the “ugly content that pervades the social media” on tech companies and on algorithms. As he puts it, “Social media churns out information that’s been highly processed to stimulate not just engagement but also dependency.” By encouraging excessive and unchecked self-exposure to a mass audience, it shatters all boundaries. The result is discord, not harmony. An earlier book also warned of a world of fractured attention.In The Lonely Century, economist Noreena Hertz had a different focus, but she also addressed the harmful effects of communication technology and social media. She assigned a central role to social media and smartphones in making people “more angry and tribal”. Drawing on research, she argued that technology and social media were also fuelling a global loneliness crisis, both personal and political. Smartphones “fragment our attention”, estrange us from people and “create a splintered self”. Hertz saw social media trapping people into isolated digital bubbles and creating a meaner, more aggressive world. This is evident in trolling and other forms of online abuse. As a result, she urged the acknowledgement of the dangers of “tech addiction” and making social media platforms accountable. Communication technology has brought immense benefits to society. At the same time, it has involved serious unintended consequences. Where there is promise there is also peril. Managing the negative effects of new technologies remains a difficult challenge without easy solutions. With artificial intelligence the risk is even greater as it is growing much faster than our ability to control it. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: International law prevails
articles.content: IN its recent press release on ‘The Indus Waters Western Rivers Arbitration (Pakistan vs India), PCA Case No. 2023-01’, the Permanent Court of Arbitration hasdelivered an award in favour of Pakistan. The award, issued on Aug 31, 2026, strongly vindicates Pakistan’s position, which it has consistently maintained in diplomatic forums and in the international media. It illustrates that the principles of international law firmly support Pakistan’s case. Established in 1899, The Hague-based PCA is one of the world’s oldest institutions for the peaceful resolution of international disputes. It has earned considerable international standing for the integrity of its proceedings, the quality of its decisions and the calibre of the jurists who serve on its tribunals. It shares its premises with the International Court of Justice (ICJ). Those who authored this verdict — the details of which will be made public soon — were selected under the procedure prescribed in Annexure G (Court of Arbitration) to the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), which requires arbitrators to be well versed in international law. Accordingly, the PCA is chaired by Prof Sean D. Murphy (US), a prominent international law scholar and practitioner. He sits alongside Prof Wouter Buytaert (Belgium), a specialist in hydrology and water resources; Prof Jeffrey P. Minear (US), an experienced legal practitioner; Judge Awn Shawkat Al-Khasawneh (Jordan), a former ICJ judge; and Dr Donald Blackmore (Australia), an expert in water-resource management and policy. Pakistan had initiated proceedings, saying, “Look, the continued construction of two Indian hydropower projects violates the engineering requirements laid down in Annexes D and E of the IWT”. These requirements had been designed to ensure that water flowing to the lower riparian was not obstructed by engineering deviations in upstream projects. The concern, therefore, was that the construction by India, the upper riparian, in territory it controversially controls and occupies, could interfere with the flow of water intended to continue downstream to Pakistan. India had sidestepped this allegation by controverting the jurisdiction of the PCA and maintaining that the matter should only be brought before a neutral expert under Annexure F as it concerns “technical differences” rather than a “legal dispute”. Notwithstanding these objections, the court continued the hearing regarding the controversial hydroelectric projects. The Permanent Court of Arbitration’s award in favour of Pakistan vindicates this country’s position. Then on April 23, 2025, following thePahalgam attack, India announced that the IWT wouldhenceforth be held in abeyance. At this juncture, the PCA, seeking to satisfy itself that it possessed the requisite jurisdiction, invited both parties to make submissions. India, however, again chose to stay away. In contrast, Pakistan has always opted to participate in strategic litigation of this nature. In both theKulbhushan JadhavandRepublic of the Marshall Islandscases before the ICJ, Pakistan overcame its initial hesitation. It chose to participate in the proceedings — a consequential decision that ensured its legal position was represented and defended before the court. The reasoning for this rests on an age-old law: if a party wishes to challenge a court’s jurisdiction, it must appear before that very court and object. Even though Indian officials unleashed venom against the PCA and its proceedings, the court’s procedural wheels continued to turn. Eventually, it gave the present award, which destroyed New Delhi’s political basis for holding the IWT in abeyance. The court approached the matter with considerable care. Rather than treating India’s refusal to participate as an opportunity to proceed on Pakistan’s case alone, it independently examined the legal arguments and factual circumstances that might have supported India’s position on placing the IWT in abeyance. The court went so far as to consider material available in the public domain, including statements by Indian officials explaining the reasons advanced for India’s decision. The PCA then turned to the possible legal grounds on which India might seek to justify placing the treaty in abeyance. It examined whether the circumstances surrounding the IWT had fundamentally changed since 1960, taking into account demographic shifts, India’s growing demand for clean energy, advances in dam technology, and the effects of climate change. None, in the court’s view, met the demanding threshold required under international law to justify suspending or terminating a treaty. The PCA also considered India’s allegation that Pakistan’s frequent invocation of the dispute-resolution process constituted a material breach. Here too, the argument did not hold, and India could not establish a material breach on these grounds. The court held that this type of treaty couldn’t be treated as suspended even during armed conflict. Most importantly, it found that the IWT was intact and remained binding on both sides. Allegations of cross-border terrorism against Pakistan have long occupied a prominent place in India’s political discourse. India expressly relied upon it in its April 2025 communication placing the IWT in abeyance, and alleging that Pakistan’s support for terrorism had undermined the basis on which the IWT could continue to operate. The PCA press release states that the court took this allegation extremely seriously, yet came to the conclusion that the act of terrorism was extraneous to the IWT and did not pertain to the treaty framework. The PCA went on to say that even if terrorism allegations against Pakistan were true, they would not be valid grounds for breaching the IWT. This was a very significant finding from Pakistan’s perspective, and it exposed the absurdity of Indian arguments against Pakistan, based on the latter’s unproved responsibility for the acts of terrorism. The court’s interim measures effectively halt further construction and concreting by India while the neutral expert continues his examination of technical issues. Until that process is completed, India is expected to stop any work that could prejudice the proceedings or alter the position on the ground. We can discuss the consequences of any failure to comply — as well as the wider implications of the ruling — once the detailed award is released. After the PCA’s verdict, the legal position is very clear: if you try to bring in political issues or issues extraneous to the IWT — which is a technical treaty — and such objections are taken up by any objective forum, defeat will be the writing on the wall — and that is what has happened with the Indian side. The writer is a former caretaker law minister.
articles.author: Ahmer Bilal Soofi

articles.title: Dystopia now?
articles.content: IT’S a little disturbing to live long enough to see fictional dystopias become reality. Take Ray Bradbury’s Fahrenheit 451 — published in 1953 — which depicts a world in which books are outlawed and specially designated ‘firemen’ are tasked with destroying these offending objects wherever they are found. The soulless world imagined by Bradbury didn’t take shape overnight; as society became more and more fast-paced, people began to prefer their entertainment to be as shallow as possible, which led to wall-sized interactive televisions in every home constantly broadcasting bright and chaotic programming for people to numb themselves with. People wore tiny wireless ‘seashell’ earbuds streaming a constant “electronic ocean of sound” into their ears, even while asleep, effectively drowning out the world and any need for actual human interaction. What social activities remained were vapid and violent; there were places where you could go and engage in wanton destruction with full social sanction. As for schools, they were now meant only to produce “runner, jumpers [and] racers” and not thinkers. Naturally, subjects like history and philosophy were no longer needed. Independent thought was tedious and troubling and so was done away with. The best part? None of this was the result of some Big Brother State intent of anaesthetising the public; the process began from the bottom-up, with society itself demanding that literature be condensed, with classics first being reduced to digests, and then to summaries, and then finally being legislated out of existence. Seventy-three years later, you yourself can judge how much of Bradbury’s nightmare has come to pass, albeit in a somewhat altered form. Recently we learned that AI companies have been bulk-buying thousands upon thousands of old and rare books — sometimes the only remaining copies — to be scanned and fed into their machines and then shredded and destroyed because that is apparently the most efficient method available. Why old books? Because the Large Language Models have already scraped the entire internet and are now at risk of ‘model collapse’ where, because AI is increasingly relying on material produced by other AI, the quality of output is degrading. It’s like making photocopies of photocopies until the text is no longer legible. Why search page after page when summaries are available? Hence, they must turn to older, human-written texts from an age long before AI or even the internet that provide the kind of rigorous high-quality knowledge and writing that is hard to come by in these times. Once you’ve absorbed the irony of AI considering AI-produced writing as sub-par, consider the wider implications: The irreplaceable knowledge contained in these soon-to-be shredded books would now be the sole property of companies like Anthropic, whose intent it is to monopolise that knowledge and sell it to you on a meter with no way for you to discern whether the output of the LLMs you will come to rely on is factual or simply what those who write — or manipulate — the algorithms want you to believe. In that latter category falls Israel, which created a fake thinktank called the ‘Hanover institute for Public Policy’. It has no physical address or staff and its reports carry no bylines but it has nevertheless produced 124 “academic-looking reports” comprising of over 560,000 words of pro-Israeli content in just nine days, none of which are meant for direct human consumption but for LLMs to pick up and reproduce. With headlines deliberately resembling the kind of queries one asks of AI chatbots, like ‘is Israel carrying out a genocide in Gaza?’ or ‘has Israel driven Palestinians from their homes?’ these ‘reports’ are meant to be consumed by AI and then vo-mited out in response to user que-ries. Do a Google search right now and the search engine will not immediately take you to a list of websites. Instead, an AI summary will pop up on your screen. It’s convenient and often useful of course, but this new feature — one that we did not choose — has also reduced organic website traffic by anywhere from 38 per cent to 60pc. This means that smaller, but highly useful independent news publishers and information providers are seeing less traffic and thus less income and may soon cease to exist. The bigger fish in the media ecosystem can take the hit, and we already know how easy it is for the powers that be to manage those bigger fish. So why go through the trouble of searching page after page (and maybe learning something new in the process, God forbid) when easily digestible summaries are a click away? Why sit through a nuanced, perhaps hours-long lecture on YouTube when you can just read the AI summary? Why take the time and effort to think when someone else can do it for you? Why bother reading any of this when you can just watch reels?
articles.author: Zarrar Khuhro

articles.title: The fertility option
articles.content: WHY does a woman have to know today whether she will want to become a mother tomorrow? Some women want children, some are unsure, and some may never want them at all. In Pakistan, where the biological clock is often accompanied by reminders of shaadi ki umar and warnings of future regret, egg freezing remains an uncomfortable idea. Recently, US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez documented her egg-freezing procedure on social media. While many praised her openness, others criticised her for delaying motherhood. The discomfort is likely to be even greater in Pakistan, where marriage and motherhood remain deeply intertwined. A recent Dawn feature, ‘How to freeze your eggs in Pakistan’, shows that the procedure is available in Pakistan, alongside stigma and practical barriers. Rather than treating fertility-preserving technology as something to fear, we should ask what problem it is trying to solve. Several economic ideas help explain why freezing one’s eggs can be a rational response to uncertainty, without implying that every woman should do it, or even that every woman ultimately wants children. ‘Real options theory’, developed prominently by Avinash Dixit and Robert Pindyck in Investment Under Uncertainty (1994), shows that when decisions are difficult to reverse and the future is uncertain, keeping an option open can have value. Egg freezing offers a similar option: a woman may later use her frozen eggs, never need them, or decide she does not want children at all. Its value lies in preserving the possibility of motherhood without requiring her to decide today what her future self must want. But the value of keeping an option open depends on what time allows. This is where ‘search theory’ becomes useful. Marriage is a search problem: no one knows when a suitable partner will appear, while waiting can bring both benefits and costs. In Pakistan, those costs are also shaped by the marriage market. Recent research by Bashir and Nazir (2025) highlights the importance of family networks, finding that nearly half of marriages are consanguineous, most commonly between first cousins. Waiting is therefore not simply a private calculation between a woman and her biological clock; it occurs within family networks and social expectations. For a woman who wants children, declining fertility can make continued search costly. Egg freezing cannot remove the uncertainty of finding the right partner, but it may reduce one cost of waiting and give some women greater freedom to reject a match that does not feel right. The value of keeping an option open depends on what time allows. But uncertainty does not end with finding a partner. A woman may also be uncertain whether motherhood will remain part of the life she wants. Economics allows for heterogeneous preferences: one woman may be certain she wants children, another may want to preserve the possibility, and another may decide motherhood is not for her. These are different preferences under uncertainty, not different degrees of rationality. This matters because women are often asked to make reproductive decisions through the language of future regret: ‘what if you change your mind?’ Graham Loomes and Robert Sugden’s ‘regret theory’ shows how anticipated regret can shape choices under uncertainty. Applied to reproductive decisions, regret can run in multiple directions. A woman may regret not freezing her eggs, but she may also regret paying for a procedure she never uses; she may regret not having children, but she may also regret becoming a parent under pressure. The question is not how to eliminate regret, but which risks a person is willing to bear. Yet regret is not formed in a social vacuum. ‘Identity economics’, associated with George Akerlof and Rachel Kranton, argues that choices are shaped by social identities and the norms attached to them. In Pakistan, marriage and motherhood are treated as expected stages of a woman’s life. Slamat, Bracke and Ceuterick (2026), studying childless women in rural Punjab, describe motherhood as socially obligatory and find that women are expected to demonstrate mothering qualities and seek treatment to validate their desire for motherhood. In such a setting, even anticipated regret may be shaped by social expectations. Egg freezing is valuable precisely because it can give women more room to make personal decisions on their own timeline, though that freedom will remain unequal as long as access is limited by cost. Finding the right partner is difficult, and not every woman who wants children will meet that person in time. Some will freeze their eggs and later use them; others may decide motherhood is not the life they want. Reproductive freedom should mean having space to pursue motherhood, postpone it, remain uncertain about it, or reject it altogether. The writer is an assistant professor of economics at St Olaf College.
articles.author: Kulsoom Hisam

articles.title: Unending war
articles.content: WITH the world’s focus regarding the US-Iran war largely on the conflict’s geopolitical dimensions and its impact on the global economy, the human toll is often overlooked. On Sept 1, as hostilities once again flared between Washington and Tehran, awedding partyin the Iranian town of Kuhestak, Hormozgan, was struck by a projectile. A night of joy turned into one of terror and tragedy as at least five people, including children, were killed. Several were injured. It is widely believed the US is responsible for this abominable attack; the American vice-president says his country isinvestigating the incident. The tragedy mirrors the atrocity that occurred at the Minab school at the beginning of the conflict, in which over 150 people — mostly schoolchildren — were massacred, again in an American attack. These deplorable incidents indicate that the US has no war strategy; precious lives are being lost because a bruised superpower cannot admit that it has failed. The response from the highest office in the US is nonsensical; US President Donald Trump has proposedrenaming the Strait of Hormuz the ‘Trump strait’, and has claimed that America’s weapons stock is “virtually unlimited”. The latter claim is particularly difficult to believe, as several sources have said the US is running low on munitions. Many within the US system realise that dragging the war further is useless; several top American generals have reportedly told their civilian bosses that escalation with Tehran is not advisable. There is apparently great tumult within the Pentagon over the prosecution of the Iran war. Meanwhile, the effects of the conflict are spreading, as the pro-Iran Houthis have clashed with the Yemeni government over control of the strategically importantBab al-Mandeb. A high number of fatalities have been reported in the clashes. If there are any sane voices within the White House, they must ask their boss to end the Iran war immediately. While it may be humiliating for the US to admit that it failed in bringing Iran to its knees, carrying on with this disastrous war will be an even bigger mistake. American wars against sovereign states have, over the past few decades, rarely ended the way Washington has desired; the current conflict is no exception. The Islamabad MoU, which theIranians have expressed their confidence in, remains the best bet towards a negotiated settlement. If the US has a better plan, it is welcome to share it. But threats, bluster and further attacks will take it nowhere, and will drag the region into an even bigger conflict. Mr Trump must end this war of choice immediately, and come to the table with Iran to work out a mutually acceptable long-term peace deal.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Export reality
articles.content: THE FPCCI is rightly concerned over the burgeoning trade deficit that has widened by 18.1pc to $7.1bn in the first two months of the current fiscal year due to growing imports and stagnating exports. The country’s apex trade body has described the rising cost of doing business as a binding constraint on exports. A policy rate above regional rivals, costly and unreliable energy supply, and higher taxes on petrol are structural costs that show up directly in the price of exporters. This explains a good part of why our exports keep losing shelf space to competitors who face none of these burdens. But it is not the whole story. Start with the product mix. Pakistan’s exports have leaned on textiles and apparel for decades, and the composition has barely shifted even as competitors moved up the value chain. Bangladesh, for example, has pushed harder into higher-margin garments and diversified into pharmaceuticals and light engineering. Pakistani exporters, by contrast, have been content to ship yarn, grey cloth and low-end made-ups, and other commodities. Value addition was always the way out of that trap. But most manufacturers did not opt for it. The market concentration compounds the problem. Exporters that have spent decades selling largely in the same markets have limited leverage when demand softens, and no cushion when a market turns against them. Product and market diversification takes marketing spend, product development and a tolerance for lower margins — costs our industry has generally skipped in favour of the domestic market for higher pricing power and thinner competition. Though understandable for an individual firm, collectively, it has hollowed out the export base. Most exporting companies remain family-run and lack in-house expertise in global marketing, compliance and product design. Modernising means hiring professionals and ceding some control. Few owners have been willing to do this. If borrowing costs are truly the obstacle, the stock market offers a way around them. Equity carries no policy rate. Yet companies show little appetite for listing due to a reluctance to open their books to regulators or share profits outside the family. Most may simply not be investment-grade enough to survive that scrutiny. The export sector needs an overhaul on both ends: a government policy that favours exports, and real diversification, value addition and corporatisation from firms themselves.
